study.title: Acts 28 The Gospel Comes to Rome Without Deterrent
study.overview: The chapter closes the book of Acts showing God's providence at every stage of Paul's journey: the sinking in Malta, the signs of mercy among the islanders, the healing of the sick, the arrival in Rome and, finally, the proclamation of the Kingdom of God in the capital of the empire. The final highlight is not Paul's prison, but the freedom of God's word. Even in custody, he receives people, a witness of Jesus, argues from the Law of Moses and the prophets, and continues to preach boldly without anyone being able to prevent his mission.

outline.title: Providence in Malta
outline.explanation: The survivors discover that they are in Malta. The inhabitants show a rare kindness, but Paul is bitten by a viper. First the people judge him criminal; then, seeing that he does not suffer damage, changes his mind. Then Paul heals the father of Publius and other sick, and receives honor and support for the continuation of the journey.

outline.title: From the island to Rome
outline.explanation: After three months, the entourage resumes navigation and passes through Syracuse, Régio and Putéoli, where he meets brothers and remains seven days. When he arrives near Rome, brothers go to the meeting of Paul, who thanks God and takes courage. In Rome, he stays in a rented house, with some freedom, but still as imprisoned, and then summons the Jewish leaders to explain his situation and hope.

outline.title: Testimony and division in the face of Israel's hope
outline.explanation: The Jewish leaders claim not to have received formal accusations against Paul, but they want to hear from him about the Christian movement, which they know how to be challenged everywhere. On the appointed day, many come to hear him; Paul witnesses about the Kingdom of God and seek to persuade them concerning Jesus by the Law and the Prophets. Some believe, others do not, and their departure ends in great discussion. Paul then applies Isaiah's prophecy, warning about the resistance of the human heart and declaring that God's salvation was also sent to the Gentiles.

outline.title: Two years of teaching without hindrance
outline.explanation: The book ends with Paul for two years in a rented house, receiving everyone who sought him. He continues to preach the Kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ boldly, without any hindrance. The end is open, but theologically strong: the work continues, and the message cannot be imprisoned.

study.context: The chapter presents the final phase of Paul's journey to Rome, after the previous shipwreck. The text shows a sequence of welcome, travel, arrival in the city and contact with Jews from Rome. There is no need to resort to external details to understand the central point: God leads Paul to the heart of the empire so that the gospel is proclaimed there as well.
study.theology: Acts 28 teaches God's sovereignty over dangers, diseases, human accusations and limits imposed by authorities. The bite of viper and healings in Malta show that the Lord preserves and authenticates his messenger. The reception in Rome shows that the church crosses borders. Isaiah's quote highlights human responsibility before revelation: some listen in faith, others harden the heart. The outcome states that God's salvation reaches the Gentiles and that the preaching of Jesus continues despite prison. The chapter thus unites mission, suffering, witness, and victory of the word of God.

scholarViews.insight: Even in house arrest, Paul courageously proclaimed the message of the Kingdom; the final word of the chapter emphasizes that the gospel follows free and without impediment.
The passage shows that Paul, though imprisoned, was not without work: God preserved him and put him in a position to be useful, so that his apparent limitation became an occasion for good.
The outcome highlights that Paul announced the Kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ, presenting Christ as the Lord and the Savior in the midst of his imprisonment.

questions: What does Acts 28 teaches about the way God can use suffering and limitations to advance his work?
Why do some listeners believe and others reject the same message, as happens in Rome?
How does the expression without hindrance confront our tendency to measure the effectiveness of the gospel only by favorable circumstances?
study.practice: This chapter calls the believer to maintain fidelity when circumstances seem unfavorable. Instead of interpreting delays, arrests, opposition or route changes as defeat, one must continue to serve, praying, welcoming people, witnessing to Christ and trusting that God opens doors at the right time. It is also a call to receive the gospel with a teachable heart, not to repeat the resistance described in Isaiah. Where there is freedom to speak of Jesus, we must do so boldly and clearly.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not inform Paul's later outcome after these two years, and the chapter does not detail the complete reaction of the listeners after their departure.
